---
title: "Working with a database from R"
description: >
  Choose THIP tables, build a database query, and bring a useful result into R.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 57)
loadNamespace("duckdb")
registerS3method("db_connection_describe", "duckdb_connection",
                 function(con, ...) "example database", envir = asNamespace("dbplyr"))
```

[Meet the THIP data](meet-the-data.html) explains what the tables and fields
represent. This guide shows how to work with them from R while controlling how
much data comes into your session.

The examples use **invented records** from `thip_connect_example()`. To run
them, you need the optional `duckdb` package (version 1.3.0 or later); install
it with `install.packages("duckdb")` if it is not already available. This is
for the synthetic example, not the THIP connection. Inside THIP, use
`thip_connect()` for the real database instead. See [Start here](start-here.html)
for connection setup.

```{r connect}
library(thipR)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
con <- thip_connect_example()
```

## Connect and choose a table {#choose-a-table-or-a-stack}

`thip_list_tables()` lists the available tables. Here, `tbl()` points to one
synthetic yearly table:

```{r one-table}
thip_list_tables(con)
stays <- tbl(con, "nhso2567")
```

`stays` is a **lazy query**: it points to a table without downloading its rows.
Creating it may request column metadata. Adding supported dplyr operations
builds a query; printing it fetches a small preview, and `collect()` retrieves
the complete query result. Even a small preview can require substantial work on
the database.

## Where the work happens {#where-the-work-happens}

There are two places to process data: the **database** and your **R session**.
In a THIP notebook, your R session runs in the Jupyter environment, not
necessarily on your laptop. The connection `con` links the two.

You can process data in the database and bring back the result, or retrieve a
set of rows and work on them in R. **`collect()` is the dividing step**: it runs
the database query and retrieves its result into an R tibble. Before it,
supported dplyr operations on a database table build a query; afterwards,
operations on the collected result run in R. dbplyr translates supported
operations into SQL, the language the database runs.

```{r two-places, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("```{=html}", "<div style=\"margin: 0.5rem 0 1.5rem;\">",
    readLines("figures/two-places.svg"), "</div>", "```", sep = "\n")
```

For large THIP tables, a useful starting pattern is: **filter, select or
summarise in the database → collect a manageable result → continue in R**.
Collect individual records when your analysis needs them.

## Compare the same query {#build-and-inspect-a-database-query}

Both examples count the synthetic records with `sex` code `"1"`. The count is
of records, not distinct people. They use the `stays` query defined above.

| | Process in the database | Process in R |
|---|---|---|
| Work | Filter and count before `collect()` | Retrieve rows, then filter and count |
| Benefit | Can transfer fewer rows and use less R memory | Can use R functions that have no database translation |
| Trade-off | Operations must be supported by the database | Retrieved data and intermediate results must fit in R memory |

Neither approach is always faster; the query, transfer size and available
resources matter. The R-first example below retrieves the `sex` column for
**every row**. It is suitable for this small synthetic table; on real THIP,
retrieving a whole column may exceed time, row or memory limits.

<span id="bring-results-into-r"></span>

:::: {.row}
::: {.col-sm-6}
**1. Process in the database**

`filter()` and `count()` build the query; `collect()` brings its one-row
result into R.

```{r database-first}
database_count <- stays |>
  filter(sex == "1") |>
  count() |>
  collect()
database_count
```
:::

::: {.col-sm-6}
**2. Process in R**

`collect()` retrieves the column first; `filter()` and `count()` then run in R.

```{r r-first}
r_count <- stays |>
  select(sex) |>
  collect() |>
  filter(sex == "1") |>
  count()
r_count
```
:::
::::

```{r verify-comparison, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(as.numeric(database_count$n) == as.numeric(r_count$n))
```

Both return the same count in this example, but the second transfers all rows
of one column before filtering. If you need individual records, select the
columns and rows you need before collecting; count candidates first when you
are unsure how large the result will be. You can use `show_query()` to inspect
SQL for a lazy query without executing the data query.

## Choose several yearly tables

`tbl()` is a standard dplyr function for starting a query on one named table.
For compatible yearly tables, `thip_table()` is thipR's helper:

```{r stacked-tables}
admissions <- thip_table(
  con,
  tables = c("nhso2565", "nhso2566", "nhso2567"),
  .id = "source_table"
)
```

This stacks rows and adds a `source_table` column identifying their original
table. Repeated rows are preserved; the helper checks columns and types but
cannot establish that their meanings are identical across years. Stack tables
that contain the same kind of records. It can also convert specified dates.

## From a query to a study

A research workflow can move between the database and R more than once:

1. **Database:** select candidate index admissions using the study's dates and
   diagnosis codes.
2. **R session:** collect candidates and choose the entries required by the
   study, such as one qualifying admission per person.
3. **Database → R:** use `thip_window()` with those entries to retrieve matching
   records around each person's dates, then analyse them in R.

[From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html) works through the first two
steps. [Look back and follow up](look-back-follow-up.html) uses
`thip_window()` to retrieve history and follow-up records. Those records may
need diagnoses beyond the index codes; for example, an all-cause readmission
could have a different diagnosis from the index admission.

### Local cohorts and remote records {#join-tables-on-the-same-connection}

A local R data frame and a remote database query cannot be joined directly in
the usual way without copying or embedding the local data. In this read-only
workflow, don't use `copy_to()`, `compute()` or automatic copying to create
tables on the database. `thip_window()` instead plans person-specific windows
from a local entry table and queries matching records when you `collect()`.
Its result still needs to fit in R memory.

## Things to know before moving on

### The example is DuckDB; THIP is ClickHouse {#the-example-is-duckdb-thip-is-clickhouse}

The example database uses DuckDB; THIP uses ClickHouse. The same dplyr code can
behave differently. For example, converting malformed age text with
`as.integer()` can yield `NA` in the example but an error on THIP. A
`left_join()` run on the database also differs: where a row has no match, the
example gives `NA` in the other table's columns, while THIP's ClickHouse gives
empty text and 0, so `is.na()` does not find them. On THIP, test for `""` or
0, or collect both results and join them in R. Check values, missingness and
conversions before relying on results; [Check before you
trust](data-checks.html) shows how.

For general syntax, see the upstream [dplyr introduction](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/dplyr.html),
[dbplyr introduction](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/dbplyr.html),
[dplyr guide to joins](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/two-table.html),
and [dbplyr function translation](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/translation-function.html).

When finished, close the connection:

```{r disconnect}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

Next: [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html) develops a study
example step by step.
